1.pericope_label: The word of the Lord that came to Joel the son of Pethuel. Hear this, ye old men, and give ear, all ye inhabitants of the land. Hath this been in your days, or even in the days of your fathers? Tell ye your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation. That which the palmerworm hath left hath the locust eaten; and that which the locust hath left hath the cankerworm eaten; and that which the cankerworm hath left hath the caterpiller eaten.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the prophet's name as compounded of the titles of the God of revelation and of nature and reports that nothing is known of him beyond his father's name, and keeps the four devourers distinct as swarms, finding significance in their number; Keil and Delitzsch dismiss the traditional accounts of his birthplace as unsupported and place him among the earliest of the twelve, arguing it from a later prophet who opens with a sentence taken from this book.

Gill rejects the identification of the prophet's father with Samuel on grounds of chronology and character and passes on the rule that a father is named only when honourable; Calvin calls that rule frivolous and remarks how boldly such expositors invent a fable and allege it as divine truth, and reads the four barren years as a portent too regular to be chance.

Clarke lays out the rival dates, gives the etymology of each of the four names, and concludes against the plain reading that all four denote the same insect at successive stages of growth; Wesley places the prophecy early and takes the four for kinds succeeding one another.

Henry calls the rabbinic identification a foolish fancy, records that many interpreters take the whole for armies of men and some make the four creatures the four monarchies, and draws the rule that those who outdo their predecessors in sin may expect sorer judgments.

positions.position: Among the earliest of the twelve, since a later prophet opens his book with a sentence taken from this one.
Probably under Manasseh, the collateral circumstances favouring it, though others put him after the fall of the northern kingdom or make him a contemporary of Hosea.
In the latter end of a northern reign and in the days of a king of Judah.
One insect at four successive stages of growth, the names denoting its progress rather than distinct kinds.
Four distinct swarms; the number itself recalls the four sore judgments and four foreign invasions.
Four kinds succeeding one another.
Four successive barren years, the sequence rather than the species being the portent.
Armies of men, some making them the four monarchies that in turn oppressed the people.

outliers.claim: Calls the rule that a prophet's father is named only when honourable frivolous, observing that when no reason appears to these expositors they invent some fable and allege it as a divine truth.

themes: The word of the Lord that came to Joel the son of Pethuel.
Hear this, ye old men, and give ear, all ye inhabitants of the land. Hath this been in your days, or even in the days of your fathers?
Tell ye your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation.
That which the palmerworm hath left hath the locust eaten; and that which the locust hath left hath the cankerworm eaten; and that which the cankerworm hath left hath the caterpiller eaten.

5.pericope_label: Awake, ye drunkards, and weep; and howl, all ye drinkers of wine, because of the new wine; for it is cut off from your mouth. For a nation is come up upon my land, strong, and without number, whose teeth are the teeth of a lion, and he hath the cheek teeth of a great lion. He hath laid my vine waste, and barked my fig tree: he hath made it clean bare, and cast it away; the branches thereof are made white.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the waking as a waking from the insensibility wine causes, notes that the word for nation here is not the one used of ants and conies but one suggestive of foreign attack, and hears in the possessive vine a mercy remembered in wrath; Keil and Delitzsch mark only the turn by which the whole nation is called to mourn.

Gill reads the nation as locusts named from their numbers and an emblem of the coming invaders, and takes the wasted vine as the same emblem; Calvin refuses the common view that these verses describe the locusts more fully and holds that a distinct judgment, war after famine, is recorded, and denies that the vine here means the church.

Clarke supplies the agricultural fact that ruin among vines prevents the vintage for years after, dismisses the attempts to identify the four creatures with four attacks or powers or kings as arbitrary and precarious, and notices the plays on words in which the prophet delights; Wesley holds insects and invaders together and applies the word strong to either.

debates.question: Do these verses describe the locusts or a further judgment?

positions.position: A fuller description of the locusts already spoken of.
A distinct judgment: war coming on a people already worn out with famine.
Real locusts, with a double prophecy of invasion admitted alongside.

debates.question: What does the phrase my vine mean?

positions.position: A mercy remembered in wrath: it is his own vine, his own people, and the affliction is painful to him.
Not the church, as the same figure is elsewhere: God calls everything in that land his own, and the phrase accuses, since vines left to the spoiler prove he no longer rules there.
The vines literally spoiled, an emblem of the invaders wasting the land.

outliers.claim: Dismisses the whole enterprise of matching the four creatures to four attacks, four hostile powers or four named kings with the remark that of such similitudes there is no end, and the best of them is arbitrary and precarious.

themes: Awake, ye drunkards, and weep; and howl, all ye drinkers of wine, because of the new wine; for it is cut off from your mouth.
For a nation is come up upon my land, strong, and without number, whose teeth are the teeth of a lion, and he hath the cheek teeth of a great lion.
He hath laid my vine waste, and barked my fig tree: he hath made it clean bare, and cast it away; the branches thereof are made white.

8.pericope_label: Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth. The meat offering and the drink offering is cut off from the house of the Lord; the priests, the Lord’s ministers, mourn. The field is wasted, the land mourneth; for the corn is wasted: the new wine is dried up, the oil languisheth.

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the land itself the betrothed virgin who has forfeited her marriage, generalises the lost offerings as all the outward signs of communion with God, and names the three lost goods by their uses; Keil and Delitzsch supply the corrective that the affliction is removed not by mourning but by repentance and supplication, and mark the summons of the priests to that work.

Gill denies that the address continues to the drunkards and takes it of the more religious part of the people, explains the composition of the two offerings, and adds the trampling of invading horses beside the insects; Calvin addresses the whole land, explains why the husband's youth is specified, and argues that a temple left without its daily services proves God grievously offended.

Clarke attacks the rendering virgin as improper, the word meaning a young woman or bride, and says only that the devastation is total; Wesley makes the loss a death untimely rather than a broken betrothal, and notes the corn eaten in its greenness.

Henry allows either figure for the mourner and draws from it that the more we are wedded to our creature comforts the harder it is to part with them, and gives the landscape rather than the inventory, a ground with a melancholy aspect and inhabitants in tears.

positions.position: The more religious part of the people, a chaste virgin espoused and waiting.
The whole land.
The land as a betrothed virgin who has forfeited her marriage by unworthy conduct.
Those deprived of necessary subsistence, mourning as a young widow or a bereaved bride.
No: the word means a young woman or bride, Hebrew having a different and proper word for a virgin.
The figure is a betrothed virgin, not yet married.

outliers.claim: Diagnoses the failure exactly: the people felt the want in the mouth, the palate, the throat and the stomach but not in the heart, mourning as brute beasts do when hungry without asking whence the famine came.

themes: Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth for the husband of her youth.
The meat offering and the drink offering is cut off from the house of the Lord; the priests, the Lord’s ministers, mourn.
The field is wasted, the land mourneth; for the corn is wasted: the new wine is dried up, the oil languisheth.

11.pericope_label: Be ye ashamed, O ye husbandmen; howl, O ye vinedressers, for the wheat and for the barley; because the harvest of the field is perished. The vine is dried up, and the fig tree languisheth; the pomegranate tree, the palm tree also, and the apple tree, even all the trees of the field, are withered: because joy is withered away from the sons of men. Gird yourselves, and lament, ye priests: howl, ye ministers of the altar: come, lie all night in sackcloth, ye ministers of my God: for the meat offering and the drink offering is withholden from the house of your God.

schools.summary: Ellicott finds a method in the order of the withered trees, each carrying its own association, and reads the summons of the priests as the start of a national humiliation beginning with themselves, since the visitation left them nothing to offer.

Gill reads the shame as confusion covering men whose increase did not answer their labour, notes that the verb rendered dried up may also be read as ashamed, and takes the girding to be with sackcloth; Calvin defends the repetition on the ground that heavenly teaching means to penetrate the heart and not merely to be understood, calls insensibility the very summit of evils, allows two readings of the opening verb, and explains why those set over others must lead the way in repentance.

Clarke supplies an observer's account of how such swarms collect into compact bodies and strip every tree, glossing the last named as the citron; Wesley makes the shame an occasion for enquiring why God is displeased.

debates.question: How should the opening verb addressed to the priests be read?

positions.position: Either gird yourselves, which the mention of sackcloth supports, or simply hasten; the drift is much the same.
Gird yourselves with sackcloth, as two Jewish commentators supply the words.

debates.question: What is the point of the list of withered trees?

positions.position: A naturalist's inventory of what such swarms actually strip.
An ordered enumeration, each tree carrying its own association, ending in the vanishing of all joy.
A sign of wrath whose force is lost on men who feel their calamities without understanding whose hand inflicts them.

outliers.claim: Defends the prophet's repetition on the principle that heavenly teaching does not intend merely that what is said be understood but means to penetrate the heart, so that the word consists not of doctrine only but of exhortations, threatenings and reproofs.

themes: Be ye ashamed, O ye husbandmen; howl, O ye vinedressers, for the wheat and for the barley; because the harvest of the field is perished.

The vine is dried up, and the fig tree languisheth; the pomegranate tree, the palm tree also, and the apple tree, even all the trees of the field, are withered: because joy is withered away from the sons of men.

Gird yourselves, and lament, ye priests: howl, ye ministers of the altar: come, lie all night in sackcloth, ye ministers of my God: for the meat offering and the drink offering is withholden from the house of your God.

14.pericope_label: Sanctify ye a fast, call a solemn assembly, gather the elders and all the inhabitants of the land into the house of the Lord your God, and cry unto the Lord, Alas for the day! for the day of the Lord is at hand, and as a destruction from the Almighty shall it come. Is not the meat cut off before our eyes, yea, joy and gladness from the house of our God?

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the word for solemn assembly strictly means a festival day of relief from work, allows the marginal day of restraint from its root, and records the threefold repetition of the opening cry with the alliteration the translation loses; Keil and Delitzsch rule that the cry is the prophet's own words and not what the priests are told to say, and explain the coming day as bringing down everything that has exalted itself.

Gill addresses the command to the priests whose business it was to appoint the day and takes the coming day as heavier judgments of which these were a presage; Calvin explains why the day is called the Lord's, since while he bears with men he seems not to rule at all, and presses that it is near in order to stop the people's procrastination, and charges them with being blind in the midst of light.

Clarke would translate the term a time of restraint, defines the fast as total abstinence from food and secular employment, and infers from the standing temple that the prophecy preceded the captivity; Wesley describes the day as set apart to confess sin and sue out pardon, and makes the coming trouble conditional on repentance.

Henry works out what such a day required and why, that the abstaining owns unworthiness of necessary food and mortifies the body, that it was seasonable when God was taking their food away, and that since all shared the national guilt all must join in the repentance.

debates.question: Whose words is the cry that follows?

positions.position: The prophet's own, justifying the appeal just made; there is no need to supply a word of introduction as some versions do.
What the assembled people are to cry, the coming day being heavier judgments than the present ones.

debates.question: How should the term rendered solemn assembly be understood?

positions.position: A time of restraint, that is, total abstinence from food and from all secular employment.
Strictly a festival day of gathering and relief from work, here turned to a fast; the root allows a day of restraint.

outliers.claim: Explains the phrase the day of the Lord as the day on which he stretches out his hand to judge, since while he spares men his face seems hidden and he seems not to govern the world at all.

themes: Sanctify ye a fast, call a solemn assembly, gather the elders and all the inhabitants of the land into the house of the Lord your God, and cry unto the Lord,
Alas for the day! for the day of the Lord is at hand, and as a destruction from the Almighty shall it come.
Is not the meat cut off before our eyes, yea, joy and gladness from the house of our God?

17.pericope_label: The seed is rotten under their clods, the garners are laid desolate, the barns are broken down; for the corn is withered. How do the beasts groan! the herds of cattle are perplexed, because they have no pasture; yea, the flocks of sheep are made desolate. O Lord, to thee will I cry: for the fire hath devoured the pastures of the wilderness, and the flame hath burned all the trees of the field. The beasts of the field cry also unto thee: for the rivers of waters are dried up, and the fire hath devoured the pastures of the wilderness.

schools.summary: Ellicott records that several words in the verse occur nowhere else so that the ancient versions vary, offers three explanations of the fire that devoured the pastures, and sets the beasts' echo of the prophet's cry against the silence of man; Keil and Delitzsch give the closing verses plainly without comment.

Gill puts drought and insects together as the cause of the famine and takes the crying of the beasts as a rebuke to those who did not call on God at all; Calvin infers a long sterility from the useless storehouses, makes the groaning of the cattle a comparison shaming the people, reads the prophet's cry as a withdrawal from a people touched by neither shame nor fear, and names the crying of the beasts as personification.

Clarke hears the animals in the sound of the words themselves, allows either drought or insects for the fire, and grounds the resolution to cry in the fact that God alone can remove such a calamity; Wesley explains the ruined storehouses by the discouragement of their owners and says the beasts have a voice to cry as well as an eye to look up.

debates.question: What is the fire that devoured the pastures?

positions.position: Either a drought or the insects, since ground they have passed over looks as though flame had consumed it.
Spontaneous combustion from the heat, or fires set to exterminate the swarms, or the burnt appearance left behind.
Whatever the cause, the report is unusual because the pastures named are cool moist uplands that stay green through the greatest heats.

debates.question: In what sense do the beasts cry to God?

positions.position: Plainly: they have a voice to cry as well as an eye to look up.
They echo the prophet's cry while man as yet seems dumb.
By personification only, which cannot properly be said of beasts, though their noise under famine is such calling as their nature admits.
In their way, and the mention rebukes those who had no sense of the judgment.

outliers.claim: Reads the prophet's turn to prayer as an act of withdrawal: seeing that he succeeded less than he expected, he leaves the people and cries to God himself, refusing to howl as profane men do.

themes: The seed is rotten under their clods, the garners are laid desolate, the barns are broken down; for the corn is withered.
How do the beasts groan! the herds of cattle are perplexed, because they have no pasture; yea, the flocks of sheep are made desolate.
O Lord, to thee will I cry: for the fire hath devoured the pastures of the wilderness, and the flame hath burned all the trees of the field.
The beasts of the field cry also unto thee: for the rivers of waters are dried up, and the fire hath devoured the pastures of the wilderness.
